entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8115"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen12634" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1-Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:1-17</reference>.<div eID="gen12634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8115"/>1. Praise of true wisdom continued (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ec 7:11</reference>, &c.). "Who" is to be accounted "equal to the wise man? ... Who (like him) knoweth the interpretation" of God's providences (for example, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ec 7:8</reference>, 13, 14), and God's word (for example, see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ec 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.6">Pr 1:6</reference>)?<div eID="gen12635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">face to shine--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ec 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.15">Ac 6:15</reference>). A sunny countenance, the reflection of a tranquil conscience and serene mind. Communion with God gives it (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Ex 34:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen12636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boldness--</hi>austerity.<div eID="gen12637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">changed--</hi>into a benign expression by true wisdom (religion) (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.17">Jas 3:17</reference>). Maurer translates, "The shining (brightness) of his face is doubled," arguing that the Hebrew noun for "boldness" is never used in a bad sense (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>). Or as Margin, "strength" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ec 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>). But the adjective is used in a bad sense (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">De 28:50</reference>). <div eID="gen12638" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 8 Ec 8:1-17 . 1. Praise of true wisdom continued ( Ec 7:11 , &c.). "Who" is to be accounted "equal to the wise man? ... Who (like him) knoweth the interpretation" of God's providences (for example, Ec 7:8 , 13, 14), and God's word (for example, see on Ec 7:29 ; Pr 1:6 )? face to shine-- ( Ec 7:14 ; Ac 6:15 ). A sunny countenance, the reflection of a tranquil conscience and serene mind. Communion with God gives it ( Ex 34:29 , 30 ). boldness-- austerity. changed-- into a benign expression by true wisdom (religion) ( Jas 3:17 ). Maurer translates, "The shining (brightness) of his face is doubled," arguing that the Hebrew noun for "boldness" is never used in a bad sense ( Pr 4:18 ). Or as Margin, "strength" ( Ec 7:19 ; Is 40:31 ; 2Co 3:18 ). But the adjective is used in a bad sense ( De 28:50 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8117"/><div sID="gen12641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8117"/><hi type="bold">3. hasty--</hi>rather, "Be not terror-struck so as to go out of His sight." True of none save God. <div eID="gen12643" type="x-p"/>

But as God's future "judgment" is connected with the "time for every purpose" in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>, so it is here. The punishment of persisting sinners (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">Ec 8:3</reference>) suggests it. The wise man realizes the fact, that as there is a fit "time" for every purpose, so for the "judgment." This thought cheers him in adversity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ec 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">8:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12648" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8121"/><div sID="gen12650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8121"/><hi type="bold">7. he--</hi>the sinner, by neglecting times (for example, "the accepted time, and the day of salvation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>), is taken by surprise by the judgment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">9:12</reference>). The godly wise observe the due times of things (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>), and so, looking for the judgment, are not taken by surprise, though not knowing the precise "when" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2-1Thess.5.4">1Th 5:2-4</reference>); they "know the time" to all saving purposes (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12650" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 7. he-- the sinner, by neglecting times (for example, "the accepted time, and the day of salvation, 2Co 6:2 ), is taken by surprise by the judgment ( Ec 3:22 ; 6:12 ; 9:12 ). The godly wise observe the due times of things ( Ec 3:1 ), and so, looking for the judgment, are not taken by surprise, though not knowing the precise "when" ( 1Th 5:2-4 ); they "know the time" to all saving purposes ( Ro 13:11 ).

But in that war (death) there is no exemption.<div eID="gen12652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those ... given to--</hi>literally, the master of it. Wickedness can get money for the sinner, but cannot deliver him from the death, temporal and eternal, which is its penalty (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Is 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen12653" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8123"/><div sID="gen12654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8123"/><hi type="bold">9. his own hurt--</hi>The tyrannical ruler "hurts" not merely his subjects, but himself; so Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:1-33</reference>); but the "time" of "hurt" chiefly refers to eternal ruin, incurred by "wickedness," at "the day of death" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ec 8:8</reference>), and the "time" of "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">Ec 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>). <div eID="gen12654" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8124"/><div sID="gen12655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8124"/><hi type="bold">10. the wicked--</hi>namely, rulers (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buried--</hi>with funeral pomp by man, though little meriting it (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jr 22:19</reference>); but this only formed the more awful contrast to their death, temporal and eternal, inflicted by God (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.22">Lu 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen12656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come and gone from the place of the holy--</hi>went to and came from the place of judicature, where they sat as God's representatives (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.6">Psa 82:1-6</reference>), with pomp [Holden]. Weiss translates, "Buried and gone (utterly), even from the holy place they departed." As Joab, by Solomon's command, was sent to the grave from the "holy place" in the temple, which was not a sanctuary to murderers (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Ex 21:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28">1Ki 2:28</reference>, 31). The use of the very word "bury" there makes this view likely; still "who had come and gone" may be retained. Joab came to the altar, but had to go from it; so the "wicked rulers" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>) (including high priests) came to, and went from, the temple, on occasions of solemn worship, but did not thereby escape their doom.<div eID="gen12657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgotten--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Pr 10:7</reference>). <div eID="gen12658" type="x-p"/>

Weiss translates, "Buried and gone (utterly), even from the holy place they departed." As Joab, by Solomon's command, was sent to the grave from the "holy place" in the temple, which was not a sanctuary to murderers ( Ex 21:14 ; 1Ki 2:28 , 31). The use of the very word "bury" there makes this view likely; still "who had come and gone" may be retained. Joab came to the altar, but had to go from it; so the "wicked rulers" ( Ec 8:9 ) (including high priests) came to, and went from, the temple, on occasions of solemn worship, but did not thereby escape their doom. forgotten-- ( Pr 10:7 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8125"/><div sID="gen12659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8125"/>11. The reason why the wicked persevere in sin: God's delay in judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.48-Matt.24.51">Mt 24:48-51</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2Pe 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">9</reference>). "They see not the smoke of the pit, therefore they dread not the fire" [South], (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>). Joab's escape from the punishment of his murder of Abner, so far from "leading him to repentance," as it ought (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Ro 2:4</reference>), led him to the additional murder of Amasa. <div eID="gen12659" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8127"/><div sID="gen12662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8127"/><hi type="bold">13. neither shall he prolong--</hi>not a contradiction to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ec 8:12</reference>. The "prolonging" of his days there is only seeming, not real. Taking into account his eternal existence, his present days, however seemingly long, are really short. God's delay (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>) exists only in man's short-sighted view. It gives scope to the sinner to repent, or else to fill up his full measure of guilt; and so, in either case, tends to the final vindication of God's ways. It gives exercise to the faith, patience, and perseverance of saints.<div eID="gen12662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen12663" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 13. neither shall he prolong-- not a contradiction to Ec 8:12 . The "prolonging" of his days there is only seeming, not real. Taking into account his eternal existence, his present days, however seemingly long, are really short. God's delay ( Ec 8:11 ) exists only in man's short-sighted view. It gives scope to the sinner to repent, or else to fill up his full measure of guilt; and so, in either case, tends to the final vindication of God's ways. It gives exercise to the faith, patience, and perseverance of saints. shadow-- ( Ec 6:12 ; Job 8:9 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8128"/><div sID="gen12664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8128"/>14. An objection is here started (entertained by Solomon in his apostasy), as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">7:15</reference>, to the truth of retributive justice, from the fact of the just and the wicked not now receiving always according to their respective deserts; a cavil, which would seem the more weighty to men living under the Mosaic covenant of temporal sanctions. The objector adds, as Solomon had said, that the worldling's pursuits are "vanity" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">Ec 8:10</reference>), "I say (not 'said') this also is vanity. Then I commend mirth," &c. [Holden]. <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">15</reference> may, however, be explained as teaching a cheerful, thankful use of God's gifts "under the sun," that is, not making them the chief good, as sensualists do, which <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.2">Ec 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">7:2</reference>, forbid; but in "the fear of God," as <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">9:7</reference>, opposed to the abstinence of the self-righteous ascetic (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>), and of the miser (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Ec 5:17</reference>). <div eID="gen12664" type="x-p"/>

The objector adds, as Solomon had said, that the worldling's pursuits are "vanity" ( Ec 8:10 ), "I say (not 'said') this also is vanity. Then I commend mirth," &c. [Holden]. Ec 8:14 , 15 may, however, be explained as teaching a cheerful, thankful use of God's gifts "under the sun," that is, not making them the chief good, as sensualists do, which Ec 2:2 ; 7:2 , forbid; but in "the fear of God," as Ec 3:12 ; 5:18 ; 7:18 ; 9:7 , opposed to the abstinence of the self-righteous ascetic ( Ec 7:16 ), and of the miser ( Ec 5:17 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8129"/><div sID="gen12665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8129"/><hi type="bold">15. no better thing, &c.--</hi>namely, for the "just" man, whose chief good is religion, not for the worldly.<div eID="gen12665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abide--</hi>Hebrew, "adhere"; not for ever, but it is the only sure good to be enjoyed from earthly labors (equivalent to "of his labor the days of his life"). Still, the language resembles the skeptical precept (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>), introduced only to be refuted; and "abide" is too strong language, perhaps, for a religious man to apply to "eating" and "mirth." <div eID="gen12666" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8130"/><div sID="gen12667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8130"/>16. Reply to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">15</reference>. When I applied myself to observe man's toils after happiness (some of them so incessant as not to allow sufficient time for "sleep"), then (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>, the apodosis) I saw that man cannot find out (the reason of) God's inscrutable dealings with the "just" and with the "wicked" here (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>); his duty is to acquiesce in them as good, because they are God's, though he sees not all the reasons for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>). It is enough to know "the righteous are in God's hand" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>). "Over wise" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>); that is, Speculations above what is written are vain. <chapter eID="Eccl.8"/>
entries.content_plain: 16. Reply to Ec 8:14 , 15 . When I applied myself to observe man's toils after happiness (some of them so incessant as not to allow sufficient time for "sleep"), then ( Ec 8:17 , the apodosis) I saw that man cannot find out (the reason of) God's inscrutable dealings with the "just" and with the "wicked" here ( Ec 8:14 ; Ec 3:11 ; Job 5:9 ; Ro 11:33 ); his duty is to acquiesce in them as good, because they are God's, though he sees not all the reasons for them ( Psa 73:16 ). It is enough to know "the righteous are in God's hand" ( Ec 9:1 ). "Over wise" ( Ec 7:16 ); that is, Speculations above what is written are vain.
